item.title: BACK TRACKS | Part One: Lost song lives again
item.description: For more than two decades, a traditional song of the vanua of Labasa had fallen silent. It was not because the words had lost their meaning or because the melody no longer mattered. Rather, time had slowly pushed the traditional yaqona song to the background until many believed it had disappeared forever.
item.content:encoded:
For more than two decades, a traditional song of the vanua of Labasa had fallen silent.

It was not because the words had lost their meaning or because the melody no longer mattered. Rather, time had slowly pushed the traditional yaqona song to the background until many believed it had disappeared forever.

But deep within Navakuru Village, the song had never truly died.

It had lived quietly in the memories of elders who continued to practise it, preserving every word through oral tradition while waiting for the day it could once again echo through a chiefly yaqona ceremony.

That day finally arrived during the revival of Labasa’s Yaubula Day. For the first time in more than 20 years, the traditional yaqona song known as Cila na Siga Va Vula Lima was performed once again before the vanua of Labasa, restoring a treasured cultural practice that many thought had been lost.

For Tui Labasa, Ratu Jone Qomate, the moment was far more than a ceremonial performance. It was the return of an important piece of the vanua’s identity.

“After more than two decades, the traditional yaqona song performed during the yaqona ceremony of the vanua of Labasa has been revived,” he said.

“For many years this important cultural song had not been performed in Labasa, and many people believed it had been forgotten.”

The revival began unexpectedly during one of Ratu Jone’s visits to Navakuru Village. While visiting, Ratu Jone was surprised to hear familiar rhythms and lyrics being practised.

The elders had quietly continued to preserve the song despite it no longer being performed publicly during traditional ceremonies.

“What surprised me most was discovering that the elders and villagers were still practising the song. The song had been carefully preserved through oral tradition.”

Recognising its cultural significance, Ratu Jone ensured every verse was written down.

For generations, the lyrics had existed only through memory, passed from one elder to another. He said writing them down was an important step in protecting them from being lost forever.

“We took the time to write down all of its lyrics so they could be safeguarded for future generations,” he explained.

Like many Indigenous traditions across the Pacific, the song had survived because of the commitment of elders who understood that culture is carried not only through written records but also through voices and ceremonies. For Ratu Jone, the revival of Yaubula Day presented the perfect opportunity to return the song to its rightful place. Yaubula Day celebrates the perseverance of culture.

“With the revival of Labasa’s Yaubula Day celebrations, I believed it was the perfect opportunity to bring this treasured tradition back to life,” he said. “It was an occasion that celebrated not only our natural environment but also our rich cultural heritage.”

However, the revival, he said, did not happen overnight.

“As preparations began, one of the biggest challenges was encouraging young men to take part in learning the traditional yaqona song,” Ratu Jone recalled.

“Many had never seen it performed before and were unfamiliar with its significance. Convincing them to set aside time for rehearsals and develop an interest in an old ceremonial practice proved difficult.”

Ratu Jone said rebuilding the tradition required patience and persistence. “We had to explain why it was important and why it deserved to be preserved.”

Once the group was assembled, another challenge emerged. Mastering the song and its accompanying lalakai movements was no easy task.

The lalakai is the traditional rhythmic beating performed with the hands during the yaqona ceremony.

It accompanies the ceremonial song, helping to maintain its rhythm and guide the performance.

The lalakai is an important part of the ceremony, adding dignity and authenticity to the traditional protocol.

A member of the chiefly family led the lalakai, the rhythmic hand movements that accompany the traditional yaqona song.

With raised hands and carefully timed movements, he guided the performance exactly as generations before him had done. His leadership restored an important ceremonial element that had not been witnessed for many years.

“During the yaqona ceremony, the traditional song was performed with great pride and respect,” Ratu Jone noted.

“A son of my chiefly family, Ratu Roqica Qomate, led the rhythmic hand movements known as the lalakai. His raised hands and rhythmic beat guided the performance and added authenticity to the ceremony.

“It was a proud moment to witness this traditional practice being performed once again after so many years.”

Tui Labasa Ratu Jone Qomate during the Yaubula Day celebration at Subrail Park. Picture: NACANIELI TUILEVUKA

item.title: Council warns against harmful evangelism
item.description: Any religious activity conducted on school premises must respect the diversity of beliefs and family backgrounds while protecting the wellbeing, dignity, and rights of every student, says the Fiji Council of Churches. FCC general secretary Reverend Sepiuta Hala’api’api said Christian ministry in schools must always be carried out in accordance with the Ministry of Education’s policies and approval
item.content:encoded:
Any religious activity conducted on school premises must respect the diversity of beliefs and family backgrounds while protecting the wellbeing, dignity, and rights of every student, says the Fiji Council of Churches.

FCC general secretary Reverend Sepiuta Hala’api’api said Christian ministry in schools must always be carried out in accordance with the Ministry of Education’s policies and approval processes.

His comments came after the circulation of a video on social media showing a foreign TikToker singling out a Muslim student during a religious discussion because of his faith.

Mr Hala’api’api said Fiji had long-established and accountable programs for Christian Fellowship, school devotions and Religious Education delivered by trained and authorised organisations in partnership with school leaders and the Ministry of Education.

“As Fiji is a secular state, the Constitution guarantees freedom of religion and protects all people from discrimination on religious grounds,” he said.

“These constitutional principles provide the framework for people of all faiths to live together in mutual respect while allowing faith communities to make positive contributions to society.”

While proclaiming the Gospel remained central to the church’s mission, Mr Hala’api’api said “the manner in which it is proclaimed is equally important”.

“Evangelistic approaches that disregard these responsibilities risk undermining both the message of the Gospel and the trust placed in Christian ministry within schools.”

Mr Hala’api’api said Fiji’s Constitution guaranteed freedom of religion and protected people from discrimination on religious grounds.

He said the FCC welcomed the ministry’s review and supported a transparent process to strengthen approval procedures, safeguarding expectations and accountability for Christian ministry in schools.

item.title: $3.6m quarters upgrade for rural officers
item.description: The Government will invest more than $3.6million to upgrade staff quarters on Kadavu and the Central and Western divisions, aimed at improving living conditions for officers serving in rural and maritime areas. Responding to the 2026-2027 National Budget in Parliament last week, Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu said the investment would suppo
item.content:encoded:
The Government will invest more than $3.6million to upgrade staff quarters on Kadavu and the Central and Western divisions, aimed at improving living conditions for officers serving in rural and maritime areas.

Responding to the 2026-2027 National Budget in Parliament last week, Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Risk Management Mosese Bulitavu said the investment would support the refurbishment and maintenance of government residences.

“I commend the Government for its continued investment in the upgrade and enhancement of Government staff quarters, with $1.687million allocated for the refurbishment of staff quarters at the Vunisea Government Station in Kadavu and a further $1.956million for the upgrading of existing staff quarters across the Central and Western divisions,” Mr Bulitavu said.

He said the funding would allow repairs and upgrades to 33 staff quarters in Vunisea and 26 staff quarters in the Central and Western divisions, following similar upgrades completed for 29 staff quarters in the Northern Division.

“The works will include structural repairs to walls, roofs and foundations, upgrades to electrical, plumbing and sanitation systems, as well as retrofitting to improve the overall safety, resilience and functionality of these government residences.”

He said many government officers worked in challenging conditions in remote and maritime locations and required suitable accommodation.

“Many of our officers are stationed in remote and maritime locations, often separated from their families and working under challenging conditions to ensure essential Government services reach every Fijian.”

Mr Bulitavu said providing safe and modern accommodation would improve staff morale, productivity and retention.

“Ultimately, when we take care of the people who deliver Government services, we strengthen the quality, efficiency and responsiveness of public service delivery, ensuring that rural and maritime communities continue to receive the support and development they rightfully deserve.”

item.title: Public urged to boost vigilance
item.description: Citizens must become more security conscious as Fiji and its criminal activities continue to develop. Speaking to the media recently, Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe says protecting communities requires the involvement of the public, as police alone cannot address issues such as theft and drug-related crimes.
item.content:encoded:
Citizens must become more security conscious as Fiji and its criminal activities continue to develop.

Speaking to the media recently, Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Operations Kasiano Vusonilawe says protecting communities requires the involvement of the public, as police alone cannot address issues such as theft and drug-related crimes.

ACP Vusonilawe said members of the public needed to provide information and take greater precautions in their daily activities.

“The Fiji police cannot fight these issues alone,” he said.

“We need the assistance of everybody. Public, individuals to give us information and assistance in all areas.”

ACP Vusonilawe said some citizens had become careless and continued to view Fiji as it was in previous years, despite the country’s development and changing security environment.

“People think that Fiji is still the same from the previous years till now. We are in a developing country.”

He said people needed to be more aware of security measures and understand that maintaining safety required a collective effort between police and communities.

“So don’t think that police can do everything. We need each other. We do things together. So that we can provide safety in our nation.”

item.title: $1m to clear backlog on claims
item.description: The Government is working to clear 80 outstanding workers’ compensation cases worth about $1million as it prepares to shift future payments to the Accident Compensation Commission Fiji (ACCF) Trust Fund. Speaking during the recent debate on the Ministry of Employment and Workplace Relations’ 2026-2027 Budget, Opposition MP Premila Kumar questioned the drastic reduction in workers’ compensation fun
item.content:encoded:
The Government is working to clear 80 outstanding workers’ compensation cases worth about $1million as it prepares to shift future payments to the Accident Compensation Commission Fiji (ACCF) Trust Fund.

Speaking during the recent debate on the Ministry of Employment and Workplace Relations’ 2026-2027 Budget, Opposition MP Premila Kumar questioned the drastic reduction in workers’ compensation funding from $7m in the previous budget to $1m in the new financial year.

Employment Minister Agni Deo Singh said the reduction reflected progress made in settling previous claims, with the ministry continuing to process the remaining cases.

He said between 2024 and 2025, the ministry had facilitated 99 per cent of the $5,999,160 allocated for workers’ compensation.

“This included 67 school accidents and 80 are yet to be paid from March to May 2025, with an estimated cost of $1million,” he said.

Mr Singh said some cases were delayed because the ministry was waiting for probate matters and other requirements to be completed before identifying the correct dependants.

Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel added that the reduced allocation was also linked to the Government’s planned transition to a new workers compensation system under the proposed Work Care Bill.

“The $1million is to cover for the transition period, the enactment of the Work Care Bill by Parliament,” he said.

He said once the legislation was passed, future compensation payments would be managed through the ACCF Trust Fund.

item.title: Dream homes open for owners
item.description: Young Fijians should take advantage of the Government-supported affordable housing opportunities to secure long-term financial stability, says new homeowner Sulueti Tabua Chand. The 35-year-old recently moved into her own home at the Housing Authority’s Nepani subdivision after years of living with her family in Navua, describing home ownership as a lifelong goal made possible through the initiati
item.content:encoded:
Young Fijians should take advantage of the Government-supported affordable housing opportunities to secure long-term financial stability, says new homeowner Sulueti Tabua Chand.

The 35-year-old recently moved into her own home at the Housing Authority’s Nepani subdivision after years of living with her family in Navua, describing home ownership as a lifelong goal made possible through the initiative.

Ms Chand said she first became aware of the housing opportunity through friends and social media before deciding to apply after learning that eligible buyers could purchase homes through affordable housing loans with subsidised interest rates as low as two per cent.

“That sounds more better than just renting somewhere for the rest of your life.”

She said owning a home had also improved convenience for working residents who travel daily to Suva.

Ms Chand encouraged young people to consider the scheme as a pathway towards independence and security.

Housing Authority chairman Marika Sedre Luveniyali said the affordable housing model at Nepani would be expanded to other developments, including Davuilevu, Veikoba and Tavakubu.

“These projects are part of the broader vision to strengthen communities and uplift lives across Fiji,” he said.

item.title: Cooperatives pay $85k in repair, maintenance
item.description: Three mechanical harvesting cooperatives in the Western Division racked up a bill of more than $85,000 in maintenance works alone during the 2025 crushing season. Lautoka Cane Producers Association chairperson Bala Dass said repairing a machine was taking its toll on cooperatives that also consisted of large-scale growers.
item.content:encoded:
Three mechanical harvesting cooperatives in the Western Division racked up a bill of more than $85,000 in maintenance works alone during the 2025 crushing season.

Lautoka Cane Producers Association chairperson Bala Dass said repairing a machine was taking its toll on cooperatives that also consisted of large-scale growers.

“We have a cooperative that spent $30,000 repairing their machine and another almost $40,000,” Mr Dass said.

“Between the three cooperatives that is part of our association we’ve spent about $85,0000.

“This new charge will hardly cover our costs.”

Greenfield Mechanical Harvester Cooperative Limited chairperson Krishna Murti Gounder said a single part for the machine could reach between $10,000 and $15,000.

“If a manual labourer gets sick, the hospital is there to give them free service and treatment, but when a machine gets sick, the cooperative has to pay $10,000 and $15,000,” he said.

“Where are we going to get that money? Some cooperatives are running at a negative bank balance for example, me and I have to repay FDB $160,000 every year plus interest. Then we have to look everywhere for loans to make these repayments and to pay for the parts.”

item.title: Foreign operators ‘consistent’
item.description: Mechanical harvesting groups are hiring machine operators from India not by choice but out of necessity. Greenfield Mechanical Harvester Cooperative Limited chairperson Krishna Murti Gounder said locally trained operators were difficult to hire.
item.content:encoded:
Mechanical harvesting groups are hiring machine operators from India not by choice but out of necessity.

Greenfield Mechanical Harvester Cooperative Limited chairperson Krishna Murti Gounder said locally trained operators were difficult to hire.

He said the local operators were inconsistent.

“So, we bring in the operators from India because they are consistent and they can also carry out minor repairs on the machines,” Mr Gounder said.

He said this year more than 50 operators from India had been deployed to cooperatives across the country.

Lautoka Cane Producers Association president Bala Dass said it was easier to employ foreign operators.

“There is less hassle involved and we don’t have to go to their homes looking for them,” he said.
